beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Chaitanya, and this video is about how the system decides who can open which textbook. So I asked for the whole rule in plain language: every path a person can take to end up with permission, and where that decision actually gets made.

props.command: explain every way a person can get permission to open a textbook — in plain language
output: one question, asked in one place

show.event: Claude composer on the cream page, spark + 'Hi, HAI'
The ask types itself, send button arms
Running indicator, then the four result lines land — the ask lands answered

beats.note: COLD OPEN LAW: ClaudeComposerAsk is always beat 0 and shows its RESULT lines. Carries the operator's sign-in line as narration.

beats.narration_text: Every time a student clicks a textbook, something has to decide: are you allowed to open this? It sounds simple. It isn't — because there are several different ways a person can end up with permission. They might have been given it directly. They might have it because of a class they joined. Or they might just be staff, and get everything. So the system asks one question, in one place. Here's what it does.

show.event: A textbook cover and a cursor, frozen at the moment of the click
The question card resolves beneath it: ARE YOU ALLOWED TO OPEN THIS?
Three faint routes fan out behind the card — given directly / through a class / staff
The routes converge into a single terracotta-ruled box

beats.act: BODY · SCENE 2 — THREE KINDS OF PEOPLE
beats.narration_text: There are three kinds of people here, and the answer depends on which one you are. If you're an admin — you run the place — you get every textbook. No exceptions, nothing to set up. If you're an instructor, you get every textbook too, with one exception: anything marked hidden. Hidden is the setting for books still being built, still being tested. Instructors don't see those. But notice — nobody has to grant an instructor anything. Permission comes automatically with the role. If you're a student, it's different. Students don't get anything by default. Every book a student can open, someone decided they could.

show.event: ADMIN row rises — 'every textbook', nothing to set up
INSTRUCTOR row rises — 'every textbook except hidden', the exception in terracotta
STUDENT row rises, visibly empty — 'nothing by default'
Caption: permission arrives with the role, except for students

beats.note: DESIGNATED TRIM TARGET. If the reel must lose time, this beat goes before any other body beat, per the script's filming note.

beats.narration_text: And there are exactly two ways a student gets that permission. The first is direct. An admin grants them a specific book — usually because the student asked for it and the request was approved. The second is through a class. An instructor assigns textbooks to their class, and every student enrolled in it gets those books automatically. Join the class, get the books. No separate approval. Those two lists get added together, duplicates removed. That's a student's shelf. One detail worth knowing: if a class gets archived — say the semester ends — the books that came with it stop working. Access came from the class, so it leaves with the class.

show.event: Left feed appears: DIRECT GRANT
Right feed appears: CLASS ENROLMENT
Two arrows converge into one list — a duplicate title visibly drops out
The merged list is labelled THE SHELF
The class feed greys to ARCHIVED and its titles fall out of the shelf

beats.narration_text: Now the part that's actually interesting. This question gets asked at two completely different moments. Once when the student clicks to open a book. And again a moment later, when the textbook itself checks back with the hub to confirm the person really is allowed in. Two different moments, two different pieces of the system — asking the same question, in the same place, and getting the same answer. That matters more than it sounds. If those two checks had their own separate logic, they could disagree. You'd get a book that opens and then locks you out. Or worse, one that lets in someone it shouldn't. Because the decision lives in exactly one place, they can't drift apart.

show.event: MOMENT ONE — the click — appears upper left
MOMENT TWO — the textbook checking back — appears lower left
Both point at the SAME single box, terracotta-ruled
Counterfactual: the box splits in two, the two answers disagree, one reads OPEN and one reads DENIED
The split collapses back to one box — they can't drift apart

beats.note: PROTECTED IN FULL. The script flags this as the strongest 20 seconds; it must never be trimmed or dropped. Passed to shorts.py as --keep B04.

beats.narration_text: So: admins get everything. Instructors get everything that's finished. Students get what they were given, plus whatever their classes came with. One question, asked in one place, answered the same way every time. And if someone ever adds a new way to get access — a whole department buying a licence, say — it gets added here once, and every door in the system already knows about it.

show.event: Three role chips settle in a row: ADMIN / INSTRUCTOR / STUDENT with their one-line rule
All three collapse into ONE box, ONE list
A new route — DEPARTMENT LICENCE — slots into the same box, terracotta
Every door in the row lights at once

beats.narration_text: So what does this design get right, and where does it bite? Right: the same question gets asked in two different places and cannot come back with two different answers. Right again: add a new way in, and every door already knows about it. Where it bites: access that arrived with a class leaves with the class — and nothing tells the student why the book stopped opening.

artifactLines: Right — two checks, one rule. They cannot disagree.
Right — a new way in is added once, and every door knows.
Bites — access that arrives with a class leaves with it, silently.

beats.note: The script's Scene 5 is a recap, so the verdict page deliberately does the JUDGMENT instead of repeating it — what the design gets right and where it bites. That is what ai-explainer asks a verdict for, and it fits the hai register.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt: map every path a user in my app can take to get permission, then show me which two paths could ever disagree with each other. Run that on your own codebase. The first half is easy — you'll probably recognise the answer as soon as you see it. The second half is the one that finds bugs, because two answers can only disagree where the same question gets answered in more than one place. Pause here, paste it in, and count how many places yours has.

props.command: Map every path a user in my app can take to get permission, then show me which two paths could ever disagree with each other.

The suggested prompt types itself in full
